outcome: Tutte's 5-flow conjecture remains completely open since 26 January 2024; the best known general bound is still Seymour's 1981 nowhere-zero 6-flow theorem, and no case, bound, or aspect of the conjecture's own statement has moved.
summary: I searched broadly for any movement on Tutte's 5-flow conjecture (every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero 5-flow) since 26 January 2024, including any AI involvement, and found none. The Open Problem Garden page for the conjecture (fetched directly) still lists it as open with Seymour's 1981 6-flow theorem as the best general bound, and cites nothing from 2024-2026. Three items surfaced repeatedly in searches and by the triage pass, and I opened all three directly: (1) Gáborik et al., 'Manhattan and Chebyshev flows' (arXiv:2510.22234, submitted 25 Oct 2025) introduces a new 'flow-pairs' method inspired by Seymour's proof technique and proposes new conjectures the authors describe as potentially stronger than the 5-flow conjecture, but it does not prove anything about the 5-flow conjecture's own statement or move its bound -- it opens a new research direction, which is a related problem under the §3.1 rule, not a case of this one. (2) 'Nowhere-zero flow reconfiguration' (arXiv:2512.17342, submitted 19 Dec 2025, latest revision Jul 2026) studies a reconfiguration variant -- whether any two nowhere-zero 5-flows of a graph are connected by a sequence of small moves -- and proves that variant false for group and integer flows; this is explicitly a different question (about the space of solutions, not existence) and settling it leaves the original conjecture's truth value untouched. (3) A January 2026 paper (arXiv:2601.05692) proves Bouchet's 6-flow conjecture for signed graphs in the cyclically-5-edge-connected cubic case -- a distinct named conjecture about signed graphs, not a case of Tutte's unsigned 5-flow conjecture. None of the three, nor any other search result, discloses any AI or machine-learning involvement of any kind; all describe purely human, traditional combinatorial arguments. Given the frozen conjecture's own statement is about ordinary bridgeless graphs and 5-flows specifically, none of these results changes what a careful person would write in this bullet, so I classify it as open with no_change_found true, agreeing with the triage's verdict of 'none.'
competing_reading: One could argue the Gáborik et al. flow-pairs method, since it is 'inspired by Seymour's proof of the 6-flow theorem' and aimed at 'strengthening existing flow number bounds,' constitutes incremental progress worth recording as `progress` even though it does not move any bound on the 5-flow conjecture itself -- the paper is explicit that its new conjectures are merely proposed as potentially stronger, and no bound on the actual 5-flow number was tightened, so I did not adopt this reading. If a later, fuller version of that paper (or a citing follow-up) actually derives a concrete new bound implying progress toward the 5-flow conjecture, that would change the classification to `progress`.
what_would_settle_it: A paper that either (a) proves or disproves the 5-flow conjecture outright, (b) proves it for a new restricted class of bridgeless/cubic graphs (a genuine case, making it `partial`), or (c) improves the general upper bound below Seymour's 6-flow theorem toward 5 (making it `progress`), with the argument written up and, ideally, digested by experts (e.g., discussed on Open Problem Garden, in a survey, or on a research blog).
